worksheet.title: Predict With Events
worksheet.subtitle: Guess both landings, then run to check
worksheet.learning_goal: I can predict where both sprites land by following the events that start them.

parts.title: Predict the whole chain
parts.text: Good coders predict before they run. The green flag starts Bit, and Bit's last block broadcasts 'go'. Pixel starts 'when I receive go'. To predict where BOTH land, follow the events: green flag → Bit moves and sends 'go' → Pixel hears 'go' and moves. Predict both, then run to check.

parts.title: Predict — before you run
parts.prompt: Follow the events in your head. PREDICT where each lands. Bit (home 1, forward 3) will land on: ____  Pixel (home 5, back 2) will land on: ____

parts.title: Run and check
parts.prompt: Now run it: click the flag, let Bit broadcast 'go', then run Pixel. Where did each really land? Bit: ____  Pixel: ____. Did your prediction match?

parts.title: What started Pixel?
parts.prompt: Pixel had no green-flag block. What event started Pixel's script? Write it.

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: Predicting with events means following the chain: which event starts the first script, what message it sends, and which script that message starts next. Then each sprite's moves tell you where it lands.

teacher_guide.eyebrow: Teacher Guide · Grade 2 · Events & Parallel Scripts
teacher_guide.title: Predict With Events
teacher_guide.subtitle: Quick facilitation notes & answer key

parts.title: Goal
parts.text: Students PREDICT the combined outcome of an event chain before running it — the C3.2 'predict what happens when both start' skill applied to events. They must follow green flag → Bit moves + broadcasts 'go' → Pixel runs on the message, then state both landings. Predicting the whole chain (not just one script) is the target.

parts.title: Ontario curriculum (Grade 2 — C3 Coding)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential and concurrent events.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential and concurrent events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.

parts.title: Materials
parts.text: The printed worksheet and a pencil. Optional: students write their prediction on a sticky note before tracing the events with two counters on a 0-5 path.

parts.title: Run it (about 20 min)
text: 1. I DO: model predicting Bit — 'green flag, 1 forward 3 → 4, then broadcast go. I predict Bit on 4.'
2. WE DO: predict Pixel — 'it receives go, 5 back 2 → 3. I predict Pixel on 3.' Commit predictions before running.
3. YOU DO: students run the chain, compare to their prediction, and name the event that started Pixel (the message 'go').
4. Connect: 'A good prediction follows every event, not just the first one.'

parts.title: Answer key (modelled by the run-gate)
text: Ex 2 (run) — the run confirms Bit on 4 and Pixel on 3; matching predictions.
Ex 3 — Pixel was started by the broadcast message 'go' (its 'when I receive go' hat).
Chain note: the green flag only directly starts Bit; Pixel's start depends on Bit's broadcast, so the prediction must include the message step.

parts.title: Watch for & differentiate
text: Common error: predicting only Bit — the prediction must cover both, including the message-triggered Pixel.
Common error: thinking Pixel starts on the green flag — it starts on the 'go' message Bit sends.
Simplify: predict Bit fully and run it, then predict Pixel and run it, before combining.
Extend: ask what Pixel would do if Bit's broadcast block were removed (Pixel never starts, stays on 5).
Success indicator: the child predicts Bit 4 and Pixel 3, confirms by running, and names the 'go' message as Pixel's trigger.
